evidence.claim: Pines and hardwoods line a reservoir along the Texas border
evidence.quote: The largest manmade lake in the South, Toledo Bend Reservoir is surrounded by some of Louisiana’s most impressive pines and hardwoods. The Toledo Bend Forest Scenic Byway lies in west-central Louisiana along the state’s border with Texas.

evidence.claim: The Toledo Bend Forest Scenic Byway follows rolling country beside the reservoir on Louisiana’s Texas border, through pines and hardwoods.
evidence.quote: The Toledo Bend Forest Scenic Byway lies in west-central Louisiana along the state’s border with Texas. The byway parallels the reservoir

evidence.claim: rolling country
evidence.quote: The rolling byway

evidence.claim: through pines and hardwoods
evidence.quote: Toledo Bend Reservoir is surrounded by some of Louisiana’s most impressive pines and hardwoods.

evidence.claim: Louisiana Tourism describes a 78-mile byway whose attractions combine forest scenery with lake recreation, and suggests one day for a self-guided tour.
evidence.quote: Distance: 78 miles Duration: One day for a self-guided tour

evidence.claim: whose attractions combine forest scenery with lake recreation
evidence.quote: takes in both the recreational bounty of the lake and the beauty of the forests

evidence.claim: LA 191 parallels the reservoir, crossing it several times and providing access to parks along the eastern shore.
evidence.quote: The highway travels parallel to the Toledo Bend Reservoir for its entire length and crosses the reservoir several times. Highway 191 provides access to several parks and campgrounds along the eastern shore of Toledo Bend

evidence.claim: The reservoir covers 185,000 acres on the Sabine River between Texas and Louisiana.
evidence.quote: The lake has an area of 185,000 acres

evidence.claim: The lake beside the road is the result of a joint Texas and Louisiana project for water supply, hydroelectric power and recreation.
evidence.quote: Beginning in May 1963, land acquisitions for Toledo Bend Reservoir started as a joint management project of Texas and Louisiana River Authorities.

evidence.claim: for water supply, hydroelectric power and recreation
evidence.quote: The Toledo Bend Project was constructed primarily for the purposes of water supply, hydroelectric power generation, and recreation.

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1964, water impoundment followed in 1966, and the power plant began operating in 1969.
evidence.quote: Construction on the Toledo Bend Dam, spillway, and power plant, began on May 11, 1964. The closure section of the earthen embankment and impoundment of water was begun in October 1966. The power plant was completed and began operating in the early part of 1969.

evidence.claim: The reservoir inundated communities in Sabine Parish, including homes, schools and churches in predominantly poor and minority communities.
evidence.quote: In Sabine Parish, there were several communities that included houses and other buildings such as schools and churches predominantly poor and minority, that were inundated.

evidence.claim: Begin at Logansport’s Sabine riverfront, then take US 84 east to the LA 191 connection and turn south along the reservoir.
evidence.quote: Louisiana Highway 191 (LA 191) runs 75.33 miles (121.23 km) in a north–south direction from the Texas state line west of Leesville in Sabine Parish to US 84 east of Logansport, DeSoto Parish.

evidence.claim: Logansport’s Sabine riverfront
evidence.quote: Logansport is a town in western DeSoto Parish adjacent to the Sabine River

evidence.claim: Between Logansport and the southern park, North Toledo Bend State Park offers hiking and birding beside the reservoir’s upriver reaches.
evidence.quote: North Toledo Bend State Park extends upriver with sprawling Toledo Bend scenic and recreation areas.

evidence.claim: North Toledo Bend State Park offers hiking and birding
evidence.quote: Camping, hiking and birding are popular here.

evidence.claim: Fort Jesup is a separate excursion near Many.
evidence.quote: Farther north, just off the byway near Many, is Fort Jesup

evidence.claim: Continuing south, LA 191 passes through South Toledo Bend State Park near the Texas line, where small bluffs rise above the water.
evidence.quote: with the highway crossing through South Toledo Bend State Park just north of the Texas state line near Highway 392.

evidence.claim: where small bluffs rise above the water
evidence.quote: The South Toledo Bend State Park lies on several small bluffs extending above the Toledo Bend Reservoir.

evidence.claim: The Sabine at Logansport was once an international boundary.
evidence.quote: Texas won independence in 1836, and the newly formed Republic of Texas agreed to the Adams–Onís Treaty, so the Sabine River became the international boundary.

evidence.claim: After Texas became an independent republic in 1836, surveyors marked the boundary in work that began at the Gulf of Mexico in 1840 and finished in 1841.
evidence.quote: The survey crew began the demarcation process on May 20, 1840, at the Gulf of Mexico, and work was completed in 1841.

evidence.claim: A marker was placed in Logansport.
evidence.quote: Boundary markers were placed along the boundary, that included one in Logansport.

evidence.claim: Texas annexation in 1845 ended the river’s nine years as that international dividing line.
evidence.quote: The Texas Annexation of 1845, ended nine years of the Sabine River international boundary.

evidence.claim: The town’s riverfront now has terraced grounds, walking paths, a veterans memorial and a gazebo beside the US 84 entrance from Texas.
evidence.quote: The Logansport riverfront is an entrance off U.S. Highway 84 into Louisiana from Texas. It has a terraced landscape, veterans memorial, walking paths, gazebo, picnic tables, and a pavilion.

evidence.claim: The town took the name Logansport when its post office was established in 1848.
evidence.quote: The name Logansport was given to the town when a post office was established February 28, 1848.

evidence.claim: Fort Jesup’s surviving kitchen and reconstructed officers’ quarters tell different parts of its story.
evidence.quote: Since then, the kitchen has been restored and decorated with historically accurate furniture. An officer's quarters building has been reconstructed, and now serves as a museum.

evidence.claim: Colonel Zachary Taylor established Cantonment Jesup in 1822; the post operated until 1846.
evidence.quote: established Cantonment Jesup in 1822

evidence.claim: Colonel Zachary Taylor
evidence.quote: Zachary Taylor—future President of the United States—established Cantonment Jesup in 1822

evidence.claim: the post operated until 1846
evidence.quote: the fort operated from 1822 until 1846.

evidence.claim: It was built to restore order in the Neutral Strip, territory disputed after the Louisiana Purchase.
evidence.quote: to return order to the Neutral Strip.

evidence.claim: territory disputed after the Louisiana Purchase
evidence.quote: The Neutral Strip was created after the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, from which arose a disagreement about the location of the border between the American and Spanish territories.

evidence.claim: By the 1930s, only the kitchen of Enlisted Barracks 4 remained.
evidence.quote: By the 1930s, the only remaining building at Fort Jesup was the kitchen of Enlisted Barracks 4.

evidence.claim: Residents of Many raised money to restore it and made the grounds a park.
evidence.quote: Residents of the nearby town of Many, Louisiana raised money to restore the building and turned the area into a park.

evidence.claim: The reconstructed quarters now serve as a museum; the original kitchen is a survivor of the military post.
evidence.quote: An officer's quarters building has been reconstructed, and now serves as a museum.

evidence.claim: The site lies seven miles northeast of Many on Louisiana Highway 6.
evidence.quote: The fort site is located on Louisiana Highway 6, seven miles (11 km) northeast of Many.

evidence.claim: The field kitchen is original; the officers’ quarters are a reconstruction.
evidence.quote: The original field kitchen and a replica of the officers’ quarters

evidence.claim: Small bluffs lift South Toledo Bend State Park above the reservoir.
evidence.quote: The South Toledo Bend State Park lies on several small bluffs extending above the Toledo Bend Reservoir.

evidence.claim: The park is a nesting ground for bald eagles, which feed on freshwater fish.
evidence.quote: The park is a nesting ground for the bald eagle which feeds on the freshwater fish.

evidence.claim: The land was acquired in 1979, but facilities did not open to the public until November 2004.
evidence.quote: The land for the park was acquired in 1979, but it was not opened to the public with facilities until November 20, 2004.

evidence.claim: A surfaced nature trail runs 3,000 feet from the visitor center museum to the Hippie Point Hiking Trail.
evidence.quote: There is a 3,000 ft (900 m) surfaced nature trail which leads from the visitor center museum to the Hippie Point Hiking Trail

evidence.claim: The museum’s nature exhibits explain local species and their environmental roles.
evidence.quote: It contains nature-based exhibits and dioramas designed to increase awareness of indigenous species and their role in the environment.

evidence.claim: The Hippie Point trail continues for 1.5 miles; the reservoir supports largemouth bass, catfish, bream and white perch.
evidence.quote: Hippie Point Hiking Trail, 1.5 miles (2 km) long.

evidence.claim: the reservoir supports largemouth bass, catfish, bream and white perch
evidence.quote: the fish in the reservoir, including largemouth bass, catfish, bream, and white perch.

flags: No road-construction or byway-designation history is provided by the cache. The overview uses the documented reservoir project to explain the corridor’s changed landscape; no claim is made that it caused LA 191 to be built.

Material mapped length of 354.8 miles and strip points beyond the reservoir conflict with tourism’s 78-mile route. Used tourism and the LA 191 description; moments run north to south with Fort Jesup explicitly a separate excursion.

Dropped the current unqualified claim that Logansport has the only known international boundary marker inside the United States. The cached article only says its survival is apparent and supplies no authoritative comparative evidence.

Omitted the claim that the Neutral Strip lacked law until the 1819 treaty: cache pages disagree about chronology and enforcement, including an erroneous 1921 ratification date in Burr Ferry. No treaty remedy or end-of-lawlessness date is asserted.
Current “about 78 miles” changed to 78 miles because tourism gives an unhedged number. Eagle nesting is supported; sightings are not promised.
